title: Why VLCC rates just went ballistic and how they could go even higher

Spot rates are the priciest in history on every VLCC lane following a stunning surge this week. The market is in the midst of a ‘chartering frenzy’ causing ‘seismic shifts’ in rates

SPOT rates for very large crude carriers were already at historic highs at the beginning of this week. Turns out the ceiling still wasn’t in. Rates have shot much higher over the past few days.

Spot rates are now so high that the numbers look like fat-finger typos. Nothing akin to the current VLCC freight market has occurred before in the history of tanker shipping.

“Even seasoned veterans are looking at current developments in the market and scratching their heads. What is happening is truly unprecedented,” commented Erik Broekhuizen, manager of marine research and consulting at Poten & Partners, in a report on Friday.

Spot rates spiking across all lanes

The TD3C, the Baltic Exchange’s Middle East Gulf-China time-charter equivalent VLCC index, was at $982,072 per day on Friday, double its level a month ago.

Clarksons Securities put the number on this route higher still: at just over $1m per day.

“At that rate, just 130 earning days would match the value of an average 10-year-old VLCC,” said Clarksons in a client note on Friday.

“With rates jumping significantly every day, charterers find it hard to engage with the last remaining owners in the window, and [there is] even more reluctance from those being approached with forward dates,” said Braemar in a brokerage report on Friday.

MEG indexes are in part (some would say a very large part) theoretical, because so few VLCCs are braving the Hormuz Strait, particularly after the recent flurry of Iranian attacks.

“Transits through the Strait of Hormuz are considered to be at their most dangerous state since the beginning of the war,” Signal Ocean freight analyst George Sakellariou told Lloyd’s List.

“Basically, Sinokor is the only known owner [transiting] at this stage, with a couple more less-known owners, plus producers using their vessels or Sinokor’s as shuttle tankers.”

That said, the VLCC rate trend is not just about the MEG — it is worldwide. “Owners need not enter Hormuz to earn exceptional returns,” wrote Clarksons.

“Broker lists indicate provisional Gulf of Oman [GOO]-Far East fixtures at around $420,000 per day. Assuming a 50-day round voyage and $10,000 per day in operating costs, each fixture would generate more than $20m in vessel EBITDA, around 15% of a 10-year-old vessel’s value in one trip.”

That math may be too conservative, as rates are spiking higher day by day.

The Baltic Exchange’s GOO-China index surged to $571,387 per day on Friday, up 113% week on week (w/w) and 300% month on month (m/m).

According to the Tankers International pool, Olympic Life (IMO: 9844277), operated by Mercuria, was placed on subjects on Friday for a GOO-China voyage with a laycan of September 23-25 at $601,771 per day.

The Atlantic basin market is likewise going ballistic. “The West, too, saw seismic shifts upwards,” wrote Braemar.

The Baltic Exchange’s West Africa-China index was at $410,759 per day on Friday, up 88% w/w and 280% m/m.

The US Gulf-China index was at $269,680 per day, up 30% w/w and 130% m/m.

“Today, we saw an October laycan for a VLCC out of the US Gulf to the East getting paid $34m,” said Sakellariou on Friday. “Yesterday, Brazil to the East was at almost $34m.”

Why VLCC spot rates are so high

One reason rates are so high is the fleet inefficiencies of the two main Hormuz workarounds: the MEG shuttle tanker-GOO ship-to-ship (STS) transfer trade, and the Yanbu-Sidi Kerir Red Sea detour trade.

The shuttle tanker-GOO system is tonnage-inefficient under the best of circumstances, and circumstances have deteriorated following recent Iranian attacks on tankers transiting the Omani route.

“That mechanism cannot work as ports do because there is not always a constant amount of oil coming from shuttle tankers through Hormuz,” explained Sakellariou. “Some days 10m barrels have come through, other days possibly zero. For vessels outside waiting to load, this is not exactly a full workaround. It ties up vessels more than an efficient mechanism.”

The flow of shuttle tankers loading via STS in the GOO will likely be even more erratic going forward, adding to inefficiencies.

According to Lloyd’s List Intelligence, crude tanker transits of the Hormuz have slowed to a trickle in the wake of the latest attacks, with that dropoff including Sinokor shuttle tankers.

There are also more fleet inefficiencies ahead for the already extremely tonnage-inefficient Yanbu-Sidi Kerir-Cape of Good Hope trade.

The Saudi Arabia Energy Ministry confirmed on Friday that the East-West pipeline that feeds the Red Sea port of Yabu has been temporarily shut down after multiple attacks on the pipeline on Thursday.

The Yanbu-Sidi Kerir workaround was in full swing as recently as last week. No more. The pipeline shutdown will waylay ballast VLCCs waiting off Sidi Kerir and those en route.

Also helping the VLCC rate market: the tonne-mile effect on vessel supply due to longer voyages, given the rise in Atlantic-to-Pacific trips during the Hormuz crisis to make up for lost MEG supply.

“In total, the number of West-to-East voyages since the onset of the war increased compared to before, and this ties up vessels for months on end,” said Sakellariou.

“After the West-to-East arb opened, the US Gulf sent 29 VLCC cargoes to the East on September dates, and eventually, there were not enough available vessels for Brazil and West Africa exports, with huge spikes in freight there.”

Another factor affecting rates: the Sinokor consolidation strategy.

Lloyd’s List first reported in January that the Sinokor VLCC joint venture was backed by Gianluigi Aponte, founder of MSC, the world’s largest container liner operator. MSC officially confirmed its involvement with the Sinokor VLCC joint venture in March.

Lloyd’s List reported last month that Sinokor has purchased 72 VLCCs since the onset of its buying spree in December 2025, with at least five more VLCCs scheduled for handover, at a total price-tag of over $6bn.

Not only is Sinokor crucial to the MEG shuttle trade, its outsized VLCC market share allows it to exert pricing pressure worldwide, according to executives of multiple listed tanker owners.

“The Sinokor effect is still in play,” said Sakellariou. “They have a huge number of vessels, which they prefer to keep idle rather than let the market fall. This is continuously adding to inefficiency.”

And then there is another factor driving the recent rate surge: China, which pulled back from the charter market during the Hormuz crisis, appears to be reemerging from its slumber.

Nick Watt, freight editorial manager at price-reporting agency Argus, told Lloyd’s List on Friday: “One driver that sticks out to me is rebounding demand from the world’s top oil importer: China.

“We’re seeing Chinese importers rebuild the crude inventories that their refineries have been churning through since the start of the US-Iran war. It’s this chartering activity from a need to rebuild these Chinese stocks that has been tightening the tanker market since mid-August.

“Argus prices are showing all-time highs on all major VLCC routes. It’s not just the Middle East Gulf, but it’s out of the Atlantic basin too, where elevated Chinese chartering activity has helped boost freight rates to these highs.”

Sakellariou said that a return of China to the market is “possibly the most important [factor] of all”.

Why VLCC spot rates can go higher still

“With cargoes still seeking coverage and little sign of the list easing, the market ends the week with strong momentum and no clear ceiling yet in sight,” said Gibson Shipbrokers in a report on Friday.

Where is that ceiling? How high is too high for VLCC freight?

That largely hinges on what crude buyers can earn selling refined products. As long as VLCC spot rates don’t exceed the refiners’ crack spread minus operating costs, there’s more room to run.

“Wide crack spreads are encouraging refineries around the world to process more crude, which is adding to the chartering frenzy we’re seeing now,” said Watt. “Even with freight rates at record highs, they’re still just a fraction of the crude price and well below crack spreads in most regions.”

Consequently, “freight has room to go higher”, Watt affirmed.

“Refining margins have been skyrocketing in the last few months and products like diesel have seen cracks that had been unheard of,” said Sakellariou.

“Increasing crude feedstock prices and freight prices will mean lower refining margins, at least in some parts of the world. Eventually, this will lead to increasing prices for end users to the point where it will be deemed unaffordable and demand destruction will kick in.

“This is the natural mechanism of the market and will affect freight gradually. But it seems we are not there yet.

“If crude prices keep increasing, this will happen sooner rather than later. Even if some countries continue importing due to security reasons, rather than refiner profits, it should be expected that freight will fall.”

As the gap narrows between crude and products prices, “this will decide the freight ceiling”, said Sakellariou.
